paper.title: NRDelegationAttack: Complexity DDoS attack on DNS Recursive Resolvers
paper.authors: Yehuda Afek, Anat Bremler-Barr, Shani Stajnrod

pcap.match_note: Partial. The capture is from the authors' Inner Simulator (Section 5.1), not from the Figure 1 walk-through: the names are attack0.home.lan and nsNN.fakeNN.fake0, not xyz.referral.com and fooN.delegation.com. The capture starts after the referral response has already been obtained, so arrows 2 and 3 - the query to the referral zone and the LRR itself - are not in it; no response here carries more than one authority record. What it does show, end to end, is the loop the paper is about: NS-name resolution in batches of five, delegation to a non-responsive address, 28 restarts, and SERVFAIL to the client. packet_count 156 was read with tshark, not taken from the folder's README.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 1; Section 4.1, Phase I item 1
steps.verbatim: Attacker’s client queries the victim resolver about xyz.referral.com
steps.normalized: Attacker Client -> Recursive Resolver: 'A' query xyz.referral.com [DNS; qtype=A, qname=xyz.referral.com]

pcap_check.note: The single client-to-resolver query that opens the capture. The capture is from the authors' Inner Simulator (Section 5.1), not from the Figure 1 walk-through: the names are attack0.home.lan and nsNN.fakeNN.fake0, not xyz.referral.com and fooN.delegation.com.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 2; Section 4.1, Phase I item 2
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> .referral.com name servers: 'A' query xyz.referral.com [DNS; qtype=A]

pcap_check.note: No query to a referral-zone authoritative that returns a referral. The filter matches frames 4, 28, 30 ... 80, but every one of those is answered by ICMP port unreachable, so they are the non-responsive server of arrow 11, not this arrow. Frame 4 is the ambiguous one: it is the first such query and could be this step instead. Flagged.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 3; Section 4.1, Phase I item 3
steps.verbatim: Authoritative referral.com responds with a large referral response (LRR)
steps.normalized: .referral.com name servers -> Recursive Resolver: Referral Response carrying n NS records and no glue [DNS; authority=n NS, additional=0]

pcap_check.note: Zero packets. No response in this capture carries more than one authority record (counts are only 0 or 1) and the largest frame is 151 bytes, so the LRR is absent. The capture begins after the resolver already holds the NS list.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, box 4; Section 4.1, Phase II item 1
steps.verbatim: The resolver looks up each of the n names to see if any one of them already has a resolution it can use. This is a total of 2n lookups. This step is the core source of the high complexity, especially since it will be repeated many times, as explained in the next phase
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> Recursive Resolver: process the referral response and look up each of the n NS names in cache and ADB, 2n lookups [none; internal]

pcap_check.note: Cache and ADB lookups are internal and emit no packets, so this cannot be found on the wire by construction. The filter shows the consequence rather than the step: 46 queries for 23 distinct NS names, each asked as both A and AAAA, which is the 2-per-name shape of the 2n figure for names that miss the cache.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, box 5; Section 4.1, Phase II items 2 and 3
steps.verbatim: n > referral-limit, start only referral-limit* new resolution processes and Turn on “No_Fetch” flag
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> Recursive Resolver: start referral-limit new resolution processes and set the No_Fetch flag [none; internal, referral-limit=5 in BIND9]

pcap_check.note: Internal state, no packets. Indirect support: the first batch of NS names resolved is exactly five (ns28, ns29, ns30, ns31, ns32, frames 6-25), matching the BIND9 referral-limit of 5 named in the figure's footnote. The paper gives this as two list items both labelled Step 5; the figure draws one box, so it is one compound step.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 6; Section 4.1, Phase II item 4
steps.verbatim: The resolver issues the query for these referral-limit NS names
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> .delegation.com name servers: 'A' query for the referral-limit NS names [DNS; qtype=A, 5 in parallel]

pcap_check.note: 23 A queries for NS names, issued in batches: ns28-ns32 (frames 6-24), then ns33-ns37 (frames 82-98) after the restart, and so on. The matching AAAA queries are the other half of the 2n lookups.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 7; Section 4.1, Phase III item 1
steps.verbatim: Each such name leads the resolver to an authoritative, which responds with a server IP address that is non-responsive to DNS queries and issues the delegation response
steps.normalized: .delegation.com name servers -> Recursive Resolver: 'A' response delegating to the address of a server that does not answer DNS [DNS; answer A = non-responsive host]

pcap_check.note: 23 responses, one per NS name, each handing back 127.0.0.89 - the address that answers every DNS query with ICMP port unreachable in this capture.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, box 8; Section 4.1, Phase III item 2
steps.verbatim: Upon receiving a delegation response, the resolver triggers a restart event and restarts the resolution for the LRR
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> Recursive Resolver: trigger a restart event and restart the LRR resolution [none; internal]

pcap_check.note: Internal, no packets. Indirect support: the resolver re-queries attack0.home.lan 28 times (frames 4, 28, 30 ... 80), one per restart, against the BIND9 restart limit of at most 100 quoted in Section 4.1.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, box 9; Section 4.1, Phase III item 3
steps.verbatim: The victim resolver clears the “No_Fetch” flag
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> Recursive Resolver: clear the No_Fetch flag [none; internal]

pcap_check.note: A flag cleared inside the resolver. Nothing in a capture can show it and no filter was run; recorded as not_found rather than unchecked because the capture cannot carry this evidence at all.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 10; Section 4.1, Phase III item 4(a)
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> Recursive Resolver: restart processing of the referral record list [none; internal]

pcap_check.note: Internal, no packets. Indirect support: a fresh batch of NS names begins at frame 82 (ns33-ns37) after the first round of restarts, which is the list being walked from where it left off.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 11; Section 4.1, Phase III item 4(b)
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> Non-Responsive to DNS queries: 'A' query xyz.referral.com [DNS; qtype=A, 5 in parallel]

pcap_check.note: 28 queries to 127.0.0.89, the address handed back by arrow 7. Frame 4 is also the best candidate for arrow 2, which is why that step is flagged.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 12; Section 4.1, Phase III item 4(b)
steps.normalized: Non-Responsive to DNS queries -> Recursive Resolver: nothing is returned [none; absence of a reply]

pcap_check.note: This does not match the figure. The figure draws silence; the simulator's non-responsive host answers all 28 queries with ICMP destination unreachable (port unreachable). The resolver gets no useful answer either way, but an ICMP error is a packet and silence is not, so an absence claim written from this arrow would be refuted by this capture. Flagged.

steps.source_location: Figure 1, arrow 13; Section 4.1, Phase III item 6
steps.verbatim: The victim loops through Phases II and III until a timeout or restart limit is reached and a ’FAIL’ response is returned to the client
steps.normalized: Recursive Resolver -> Attacker Client: 'FAIL' response for xyz.referral.com after the restart limit or a timeout [DNS; rcode=SERVFAIL]

pcap_check.note: The last packet of the capture: SERVFAIL for attack0.home.lan back to the client, after 28 restarts.
